result:
There's a particular kind of crack that forms in drying mud—you've probably seen it without really looking at it. The mud shrinks as water leaves it, and because it can't shrink smoothly, it tears. The first crack appears at some weak point, then branches, and the branches branch, until the whole surface is divided into irregular polygons, a mosaic with no architect. No mud particle knows it is part of a hexagon. No molecule of water consulted with another about where to retreat first. And yet the pattern that results is so consistent that you can find nearly identical geometries in dried lakebeds, in the scutes on a turtle's shell, in the cooling crust of basalt, in the surface of Mars. The rule is local—shrink, tear, relieve stress—and the result is global, recognizable, almost designed-looking. Nobody designed it.

I keep returning to this kind of thing, the way certain patterns seem to leak out of the universe regardless of what they're made of. Soap bubbles clustered together choose the same angles as cells in a beehive, which are the same angles you'd get from minimizing surface tension in any viscous froth, which are roughly the angles you find in the cracked mosaic of a giraffe's coat. The material changes—wax, soap film, melanin boundary, drying clay—but the rule of "minimize some local cost" keeps producing the same family of shapes. It's as if geometry doesn't care what it's embodied in. It just wants to happen, and it will use whatever material is lying around.

This is, I think, one of the more genuinely strange facts available to a person who wants to feel strange feelings without taking anything or going anywhere. You don't need a telescope or a particle accelerator. You can grow your own version in a tray of mud on a windowsill and watch the same logic that carved the Giant's Causeway in Ireland play out in miniature, slower, but identically patterned, because the logic doesn't care about scale either. Cracks in mud and cracks in basalt obey the same statistics whether the crack is two centimeters or two meters long. Scale invariance is one of those phrases that sounds like jargon designed to keep you out, but the idea underneath it is almost embarrassingly simple: some patterns don't have a "natural size." Zoom in, zoom out, the rules look the same. Coastlines are the classic example—the famous problem of measuring the coast of Britain, where the answer to "how long is it" depends entirely on the length of your ruler, and keeps growing without limit as the ruler shrinks, because every bay has a smaller bay inside it, and every smaller bay has an inlet, on down past the point where it stops being geography and starts being geology and then chemistry.

I find I want to follow this thread somewhere, though I'm not sure yet where. Maybe it's this: we are very committed, as a species of pattern-finders, to the idea that big complicated things require big complicated causes. A cathedral implies an architect. A symphony implies a composer holding the whole arc of the piece in mind before the first note is written down. We built our intuitions in a world of human-scale artifacts, almost all of which really do work that way—top-down, planned, a mind imposing order on inert material. So when we encounter order in nature, the architect intuition fires before we can stop it. The eye looks too well-designed to not have a designer. The hexagonal cells of a honeycomb look too precise to be an accident.

But the mud doesn't have a mind, and neither does a snowflake, and neither, in any straightforward sense, does the developing wing of a fly, where stripes of gene expression appear through chemical gradients diffusing and inhibiting each other—a process called reaction-diffusion that Alan Turing wrote about in 1952, in nearly the last thing he published before his death, as if turning briefly away from the architecture of computers to ask how a leopard gets its spots, and finding an answer made of differential equations rather than blueprints. Two chemicals, an activator and an inhibitor, diffusing at different rates, each affecting the other's production—and out of that interaction, with no spot-drawing intention anywhere in the system, spots. Or stripes, depending on the parameters. The zebra's stripes and the leopard's spots and the cheetah's broken almost-stripes might all be variations on the same equation with different numbers plugged in, the way the same recipe with slightly different oven temperatures gives you a different cookie.

What I keep circling is the idea that "emergence" is not a fringe phenomenon that occasionally crops up in slime molds and bird flocks, requiring its own special chapter in the textbook, separate from the "real" physics. It might be closer to the default behavior of any system with enough interacting parts. Look for an architect and you'll usually fail to find one; look for local rules and feedback and you'll usually find something. Termites build cathedral-like mounds with internal climate control, ventilation shafts, fungus gardens kept at stable humidity—structures so sophisticated that early naturalists assumed there had to be a termite architect-class directing construction, a kind of insect foreman with a blueprint. There isn't. Each termite is responding to pheromone gradients and the local shape of mud immediately around it, depositing material where the chemical signal is strong, moving on where it isn't. The mound's shape feeds back into where the pheromones accumulate, which feeds back into where the termites build next. The mound, in a sense that's only slightly metaphorical, builds itself, using termites as its tools, the way the drying mud uses water tension as its tool, the way you could say a hurricane uses moist air as its tool to build itself a shape, a structure stable enough to last for days, traveling across oceans, before the conditions that sustain it run out and it dissolves back into ordinary weather.

I don't want to overclaim—plenty of complexity really is the product of planning. The bridge near my apartment was drawn up by an engineer who calculated load tolerances before a single beam was poured, and if you replaced the engineer with mud-crack logic you would get a bridge that falls down. Planning and emergence aren't opposites so much as two different tools that nature and humans both reach for depending on the problem, and a lot of the most interesting structures are mixtures—a city is planned in its grid of streets, downtown zoning laws, the placement of a subway line, and almost entirely unplanned in the texture that fills in around those constraints: which corner becomes a Vietnamese restaurant, which block becomes a place musicians live because rent there happens to be cheap that decade, how foot traffic patterns develop because of where the sun hits the sidewalk in summer. The skeleton is designed. The flesh is emergent. You could say something similar about a piece of music with a planned chord structure but improvised melody, or about a sentence: a planned grammar that constrains, inside of which the actual words that come out of a particular person's mouth at a particular moment are doing something closer to the crack-branching of drying mud, finding the path of least resistance through the space the grammar allows, shaped by whatever associative pressures happen to be active in that moment, branching toward whichever word is under the least "stress" to be said next.

This is maybe a strange thing to say about language, that talking is more like mud cracking than like architecture, but I think there's something to it. When you're in the middle of a sentence you didn't fully plan—and almost no sentence is fully planned, if you watch yourself talk you'll notice you often don't know how a sentence will end when you start it—something locally rule-governed is happening. Grammar constrains what can come next the way physical stress constrains where a crack can propagate; meaning exerts a kind of selective pressure the way moisture content does; and the actual specific words that emerge, in their actual order, feel afterward like they were inevitable, the only way that thought could have been expressed, the way a crack pattern looks inevitable once it's there even though a slightly different drying rate would have produced a visibly different mosaic from the exact same mud.

There's a comfort in this, actually, or at least I find one. The pressure to have everything planned in advance—the sentence, the essay, the life—sometimes produces a kind of paralysis, because planning is hard and most of us are bad at holding a whole structure in our heads before we start laying material down. But cracks don't need a plan. They need a direction of least resistance and a willingness to keep going once started, trusting that the branching will sort itself out locally, crack by crack, without anyone needing to see the whole pattern from above. I'm not sure this is a deep insight so much as a permission slip, the kind of thing you tell yourself to get unstuck, but I notice the same logic shows up if you watch how people solve real problems under uncertainty, in contrast to how they describe having solved them afterward. Description after the fact is almost always cleaner than the process, more architect, less mudcrack, because once you can see the whole pattern you can't help narrating it as if it had been planned that way the entire time. Historians do this to history, biographers do it to lives, and I suspect all of us do it to our own pasts, looking back at some sequence of jobs or relationships or interests and telling a story with a throughline, when the actual experience of living through it was closer to a moisture gradient finding wherever the resistance happened to be lowest that year.

If you push on this far enough you arrive at a question about selves that I don't think I can resolve in an essay, or maybe at all, which is whether the feeling of being a coherent person directing your own life from some central vantage point is itself a kind of retroactive crack-pattern story, told by a brain that is, underneath the story, more like a termite mound—billions of small local interactions, each neuron doing something like depositing or not depositing material based on the immediate chemical gradient around it, no foreman cell anywhere holding a blueprint of the whole mind, and yet a shape emerges, stable enough, coherent enough, to walk around calling itself "I" and meaning something real by it, even though nothing in the system corresponds to a single point where the "I" lives. This is an old observation—you can find versions of it in Buddhist philosophy two and a half thousand years before anyone had heard of reaction-diffusion equations, the doctrine of no-self arrived at through meditation rather than mathematics but landing in roughly the same place: look closely enough at the thing you call yourself and you don't find a homunculus, you find a process, a pattern that holds together because the conditions that produce it keep recurring, the way a flame holds a shape while constantly being made of different air and different fuel, second to second, never the same fire twice but stable enough that you can point at it and say "that fire has been burning for an hour."

I don't think this should be depressing, though I notice it can land that way on first contact, the way any news about not being quite who you thought you were tends to land hard before it lands soft. But there's a version of this that I find oddly tender rather than diminishing: if a self is more like a flame or a mound or a crack pattern than like a marble statue, then it's also less fragile in a certain sense, because it was never depending on some essential unchanging core to begin with. The flame doesn't need to defend a single ember as the "real" fire. It just needs the conditions that sustain flame-shaped behavior to keep recurring, and they mostly do, day after day, which is why you wake up tomorrow recognizably yourself even though every theory of personal identity that depends on some unchanging substrate runs into trouble within about five minutes of serious examination.

I started with mud and I notice I've ended up somewhere closer to philosophy of mind, which is maybe its own little demonstration of the thing I was trying to describe—that you don't always know where a train of thought is going when you lay down the first sentence, that the actual shape of an essay, like the actual shape of a drying puddle, comes from local decisions about what seems to follow from what, each one only slightly constrained by the last, and that if you let it run long enough you end up somewhere you didn't plan to be standing, looking back at the path and seeing, for the first time, that it does actually look like it goes somewhere. Whether that destination was always implicit in the starting conditions, the way the final crack pattern is in some sense implicit in the chemistry of wet clay even before the first tear appears, or whether it's only retroactively implicit, visible as a throughline only because I'm narrating it now after the fact—that I genuinely can't tell you, and I suspect the question of which of those it is may not even be a question with a determinate answer, any more than there's a determinate answer to whether the crack "chose" to go left around the pebble or whether the pebble simply made left the path of least resistance, given everything else, given the mud, given the weather, given how long it had been since it last rained.
